title: Electrochemical Molecular Dynamics within the Finite-Field Framework
authors: Krystof Brezina, Ludwig Ahrens-Iwers, Mariana Rossi
abstract: Electrochemical processes at charged interfaces lie at the heart of modern technologies and their continued improvement depends on insights into the relevant atomistic processes. However, the necessary tools to impose constant-voltage conditions in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations typically directly target the electrode charge, making their extension to methods that go beyond an empirical description of metals more cumbersome. In this work, we propose an MD protocol to realize a thermodynamic ensemble in which voltage control is attained, but which is formulated purely within the framework of finite-field simulations in 3D periodic boundary conditions. We show a derivation and implementation of such a control device, which we coin an electrostat, in the ELECTRODE package within LAMMPS. Our simulations systematically benchmark the derived theory against other established approaches, for example, showing its equivalence to a potentiostat, and quantify the importance of properly accounting for ensemble fluctuations. We find that for systems of several thousands of atoms, one obtains the same equilibrium properties with the electrostat as with a simpler constant-field simulation. The difference between the two methods only manifests itself at smaller length scales, thereby establishing practical limits for the inclusion of voltage fluctuations in atomistic simulations of electrochemical systems. The strength of this framework also lies in its simplicity of extension to first-principles ab initio and reactive machine-learning potentials.
summary: This paper introduces the 'electrostat,' a novel molecular dynamics protocol that allows for accurate simulation of electrochemical systems under constant voltage control using finite-field methods. It rigorously proves the electrostat's equivalence to established potentiostat techniques while demonstrating its computational advantages for large-scale atomistic simulations. This advances the toolkit for studying interfaces in electrochemistry.
main_problem: The core problem is developing robust molecular dynamics simulation tools to enforce constant-voltage ($\phi^*$) conditions in electrochemical systems, especially for models beyond simple empirical metal descriptions.
main_result: The authors propose and validate an 'electrostat' protocol, showing it is equivalent to a potentiostat and yields correct equilibrium properties for large systems, while quantifying the limits where voltage fluctuations become significant.
method: The work develops a theoretical framework for realizing the constant-voltage ensemble purely within finite-field simulations using a stochastic differential equation (SDE) approach.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a nanoscopic electrochemical cell, typically involving an ionic liquid electrolyte and planar electrodes (e.g., graphite). The theory generalizes standard ensembles (Constant-E, Constant-D) to incorporate voltage control.
key_observables: Voltage ($\phi^*$), Electric Field ($E^*$), Displacement Field ($D^*$), Electrode Charge ($Q^*$), and ion-association free-energy profiles $F(r)$.
important_parameters: System size (thousands of atoms), temperature ($T$), and the time scale separation between different control mechanisms.
main_assumptions: The framework relies on formulating the control purely within finite-field methods, and comparisons establish practical limits where the inclusion of voltage fluctuations is necessary.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the various simulation setups (constant V, E, D, Q) for a nanocapacitor and show benchmarks comparing the electrostat to constant-field methods, confirming equivalence for large systems.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory of the electrostat (Section II), benchmarks this new protocol against established methods (CPM, constant-E), and presents detailed simulations (Section III) on observables like ion association free energy and charge dynamics.
why_interesting: The rigorous development of ensemble control methods that correctly incorporate thermal fluctuations (like a potentiostat) into computationally efficient finite-field frameworks is crucial for simulating open quantum systems and interfaces.
